The '''Copiale cipher''' is an [[cipher|encrypted]] manuscript created in the 1700s and consisting of 75,000 handwritten characters filling 105 pages in a bound volume.<ref name="AAAS">{{Cite news |date=2011-09-25 |title=USC Scientist Cracks Mysterious 'Copiale Cipher' |url=https://today.usc.edu/usc-scientist-cracks-mysterious-copiale-cipher/ |access-date=2025-03-21 |work=USC Today |publisher=[[University of Southern California]]}}</ref> Undeciphered for more than 260 years, the document was decrypted in 2011 with computer assistance.  An international team consisting of Kevin Knight of the University of Southern California [[Information Sciences Institute]] and [[USC Viterbi School of Engineering|Viterbi School of Engineering]], along with Beáta Megyesi and Christiane Schaefer of [[Uppsala University]] in Sweden, found the cipher to be an encrypted German text.  The manuscript is a [[homophonic cipher]] that uses a complex [[Substitution cipher|substitution code]], including symbols and letters, for its text and spaces.<ref name="Markoff">{{Cite news |last=Markoff |first=John |author-link=John Markoff |date=2011-10-24 |title=How Revolutionary Tools Cracked a 1700s Code |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2011/10/25/science/25code.html |url-access= |access-date=2025-03-21 |work=[[The New York Times]] |pages=4}}</ref>

Previously examined by scientists at the [[German Academy of Sciences at Berlin]] in the 1970s, the cipher was thought to date from between 1760 and 1780.<ref name="Bild.de">{{Cite news |last=Stein |first=Sven |date=2011-10-27 |title=Rätsel nach 250 Jahren gelöst: US-Forscher knacken deutschen Geheim-Code |trans-title=Mystery solved after 250 years: US researchers crack German secret code |url=https://bild.de/news/ausland/geheimcode/geheimgesellschaft-20676926.bildMobile.html |work=[[Bild]]}}</ref> Decipherment revealed that the document had been created in the 1730s by a [[secret society]]<ref name=AAAS/><ref name=Markoff /><ref name="ACL">{{Cite conference |last1=Knight |first1=Kevin |last2=Megyesi |first2=Beáta |last3=Schaefer |first3=Christiane |date=2011-06-24 |title=The Copiale Cipher |url=https://aclanthology.org/W11-1202 |book-title=Proceedings of the 4th Workshop on Building and Using Comparable Corpora: Comparable Corpora and the Web |conference=49th [[Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics]]: Human Language Technologies |location=Portland, Oregon |publisher=[[Association for Computational Linguistics]] |pages=2–9 |isbn=978-1-937284-01-5}}</ref> called the "high enlightened (''Hocherleuchtete'') oculist order" of [[Wolfenbüttel]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Henning |first=Aloys |year=1999 |title=Eine frühe Loge des 18. Jahrhunderts: 'Die Hocherleuchtete Oculisten-Gesellschaft' in Wolfenbüttel |journal=Europa in der frühen Neuzeit |language=de |issue=5, ''Aufklärung in Europa'' |pages=65–82 |doi=10.7788/boehlau.9783412330941.65 |isbn=978-3-412-33094-1}}</ref> or Oculists.<ref name="Wired Nov 2012"/><ref>{{Cite AV media |url=https://youtube.com/watch?v=Eam0Tk-1FyI |title=USC Scientist Cracks Mysterious 'Copiale Cipher' |publisher=[[University of Southern California]] |via=YouTube}}</ref> The Oculists used sight as a metaphor for knowledge.<ref name="Wired Nov 2012" />

The manuscript is in a private collection.<ref name="AAAS" /> A parallel manuscript is kept at the [[:de:Staatsarchiv Wolfenbüttel|Staatsarchiv Wolfenbüttel]].<ref name="Uppsala">{{cite web |last1=Knight |first1=Kevin |last2=Megyesi |first2=Beáta |last3=Schaefer |first3=Christiane |year=2011 |title=The Copiale Cipher |url=http://stp.lingfil.uu.se/~bea/copiale/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111005210407/http://stp.lingfil.uu.se:80/~bea/copiale/ |archive-date=2011-10-05 |accessdate=2011-10-25 |work=[[Uppsala University]] |department=Department of Linguistics and Phonology}}</ref>

The Copiale cipher includes abstract symbols, as well as letters from [[Greek alphabet|Greek]] and most of the [[Latin alphabet|Roman]] alphabet. The only plain text in the book is "Copiales 3" at the end and "Philipp 1866" on the flyleaf. Philipp is thought to have been an owner of the manuscript.<ref name="Uppsala" /> The plain text letters of the message were found to be encoded by accented Roman letters, Greek letters and symbols, with unaccented Roman letters serving only to represent spaces.<ref name="ACL" />

The researchers found that the initial 16 pages describe an Oculist initiation ceremony.  The manuscript portrays, among other things, an initiation ritual in which the candidate is asked to read a blank piece of paper and, on confessing inability to do so, is given eyeglasses and asked to try again, and then again after washing the eyes with a cloth, followed by an "operation" in which a single eyebrow hair is plucked.<ref name="msnbc">{{cite news |author=Alan |first=Alan |date=2011-10-25 |title=Secret society's code cracked |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/science/cosmic-log/secret-societys-code-cracked-flna6C10402805 |url-status= |archiveurl= |archivedate= |accessdate=2025-03-22 |work=[[NBCNews.com|NBC News]] |department=Cosmic Log |publisher=}}</ref>

==Substitution cipher==
The Copiale cipher is a [[substitution cipher]]. It is not a 1-for-1 substitution but rather a [[homophonic cipher]]: each ciphertext character stands for a particular plaintext character, but several ciphertext characters may encode the same plaintext character. For example, all the unaccented Roman characters encode a space. Seven ciphertext characters encode the single letter "e". In addition, some ciphertext characters stand for several characters or even a word. One ciphertext character ("†") encodes "sch", and another encodes the secret society's name.<ref name="Uppsala"/><ref name="msnbc"/>

==Decryption method==
A machine translation expert, Knight approached language translation as if all languages were ciphers, effectively treating foreign words as symbols for English words.  His approach, which tasked an [[expectation-maximization algorithm]] with generating every possible match of foreign and English words, enabled the algorithm to figure out a few words with each pass.  A comparison with 80 languages confirmed that the original language was likely German, which the researchers had guessed based on the word "Philipp," a German spelling.  Knight then used a combination of intuition and computing techniques to decipher most of the code in a few weeks.  Megyesi later realized that a particular symbol meant "eye", and Schaefer connected that discovery to the Oculists.

==The Oculists==
The Oculists were a group of [[Ophthalmology|ophthalmologists]] led by Count Friedrich August von Veltheim (father of [[August Ferdinand von Veltheim]]), who died in April 1775.  The Philipp 1866 Copiales 3 document, however, appears to suggest that the Oculists, or at least Count Veltheim, were a group of [[Freemasons]] who created the Oculist society in order to pass along the Masonic rites<ref name="Wired Nov 2012">{{cite magazine |last=Shactman |first=Noah |author-link=Noah Shachtman |date=2012-11-16 |title=They Cracked This 250-Year-Old Code, and Found a Secret Society Inside |url=https://www.wired.com/dangerroom/2012/11/ff-the-manuscript/all/ |url-access=subscription |access-date=2013-11-02 |magazine=[[Wired (magazine)|Wired]] |pages=210–218 |volume=20 |issue=12 |accessdate=}}</ref><ref name="The Scottish Rite of Freemasonry March/April 2012">{{cite web |url=https://scottishrite.org/about/media-publications/journal/article/the-copiale-cipher-an-early-german-masonic-ritual-unveiled/ |title=The Copiale Cipher: An Early German Masonic Ritual Unveiled |last=James D. Hodgkins |date=April 2012 |website=scottishrite.org |accessdate=1 July 2018}}</ref> which had recently been [[Papal ban of Freemasonry#Original prohibition|banned]] by [[Pope Clement XII]].
